new_entities.name: Heavy cycling in men
aliases: bicycling five hours per week or more
new_entities.description: Regular high-volume bicycling or cycling training in men before conception.

new_entities.name: Sperm concentration
new_entities.description: The concentration of spermatozoa in semen, usually expressed as millions per milliliter.

edges.effect_quant: The anchor fertility-clinic cohort found that bicycling at least five hours per week was associated with nearly doubled odds of low sperm concentration (OR 1.92, 95% CI 1.03-3.56). Review-level evidence also suggests cycling is one of the specific sports most consistently linked to lower concentration, but the broader physical-activity literature is not uniformly negative.
edges.population: men of reproductive age who engage in regular high-volume bicycling or endurance cycling
edges.mechanism: Heavy cycling may lower sperm concentration through repeated perineal compression, local heat buildup, and prolonged saddle pressure, potentially combined with endurance-energy stress in more serious cyclists. That mechanism is more specific than exercise in general, which is why cycling can look less favorable than other physical activity patterns.
edges.summary: The most conservative claim is that heavy bicycling is a plausible sperm-concentration risk factor, not that all cycling is harmful. The negative signal appears mainly at higher weekly volumes and should not be generalized to casual riding.
edges.caveats: Most studies are observational and may not fully separate cycling volume from clothing, saddle design, recovery state, or other endurance-training habits. The literature supports caution at higher volumes, but it does not justify treating all cycling as an infertility hazard.

evidence.citation: Wise LA et al 2011 Fertil Steril
evidence.notes: Physical activity and semen quality among men attending an infertility clinic.
